blocks.x: Hi Bill, this is Floyd Levin in Los Angeles. This is the 25th of July 1969 and shortly I expect Barney Begard over, at which time I will supply the questions and hopefully he'll come up with some of the answers to help you on your quest for information about Jelly Roll Morton. Okay, we've just played the Victor Trio session, Barney. I assume that you have some memories about that session. Yeah, I was really surprised. I thought I played more than I do now. That's going back, what, 40 years? Yes, it is. Could you pinpoint the date? No, I couldn't. I really couldn't. The only time I think that I made this date with Jelly was in New York around 1928 or 27, something like that. Well, that's pretty accurate. They pinpointed it as December 17, 1929 in the discography. That's pretty close. But was it for sure New York? Yeah, New York. That's when I made it with him. No, I made it in Chicago. Well, there's some question. No, I made it in Chicago. I'll tell you how I made it. Because Simeon was his main, Omar Simeon was his main clarinetist. I mean, he loved the guy. But Simeon went with Charlie Elgar in Milwaukee. Yeah. And so he wanted to make a date. And so he asked me to make it. And I was working with King Oliver at the time. And we made the date then. Well, you hadn't joined Duke yet at this time? Oh, no. No, no. When did you join Duke? I joined Duke in 27. 27. Well, this is 29, Barney. It's 29? This is 29. Well, now let me just say this. As far as the information in the discographies are concerned, this date took place on December 17, 1929. But perhaps your memory would indicate that the discographies are wrong. If it was before 20, was it for sure when you were with Oliver? Let me think now, truthfully. No, I think they're right. It's 29. Because I joined Duke in 27. And he came to New York at just about that time. And he was trying to get a job, get a band together. Morton was, you mean? Yeah. Jelly Roll. Jelly Roll was trying to get a band together. And he finally got a job. It was 125th and 7th Avenue. I'll never forget. He got the job. He talked himself into the job and talked himself out of the job. Oh, he was quite a character, you know. And sometimes, you know, like the old Lafayette Theater, that was around 123rd Street. It was a famous theater at that time. And you'd see a crowd on the corner. And you'd think that something really happened. Jelly and Chick Webb was arguing like mad. I mean, it was really funny. I mean, everybody got a big kick out of it. And that's the way it went for quite a while. But Jelly was a fantastic man. He was really fantastic. See, I heard of him in New Orleans when he used to work for Lulu White. That was a house of real repute. But they had a big room where the people, you know, the customers, you know, before they had anything to go in for them, that they would entertain them and they'd buy drinks for the girls and all that sort of business. Well, I heard of all that. But I've never met Jelly until I went to Chicago. You did meet Jelly in Chicago. Yes, I did. Well, perhaps you met him when you were with Oliver. I did. The reason I mention that, I have a note here that Bill Russell has given me where he mentions that Jelly Roll's sister who lives in New Orleans, Mrs. Frances Mouton Oliver. She tells him about visiting Chicago in 1925. Yeah. And Jelly took her to the plantation on 35th Street to hear the Oliver Band. Right. And you were in the band at the time with a lot of other New Orleans musicians. Right. It was Albert Nicholas and Paul Barberin. And who else was in it? Bud Scott. That's right. In fact, she even told Bill about the watermelon decorations on the ceiling. Do you remember that? Yeah, sure. This is in the plantation. Well, now, was that the first time that you saw Oliver? That's the first time I met Jelly Roll. I met Jelly Roll, yeah. Yeah. That's the first time I met Jelly. And that would be about 1925. Just about. And Jelly, you know, he was so fantastic. He used to have a diamond in his tooth. Yeah. Did you ever hear about that? Yes, I did. And the guy, the thing about Jelly, you know, when he wanted money, it was no problems. He and Melrose was like this, like brothers. Melrose, the publisher. Yeah. So any time he wanted money, he'd go to Melrose and get a thousand dollars, and in those days it was a lot of money. Sure. And he would tell Melrose, he'd go to Melrose, and he would tell Melrose, I'll write you a tune. We'll make up for it. And he'd go there, he wrote up Milenberg drawers. Mm-hmm . Duke at the time, and I saw Jelly coming up 125th Street. And he was broken down, trodden, you know. I said, hey, what's wrong with you? He said, big. He used to call me big. Big? Big. He said, big. He said, those publishers, they're smart. I said, what do you mean? He said, if they hold me down, they'll hold the rest of these writers down. That's it all, come on. I said, you'll be all right. So finally he got out of that, and then he married a gal that had a little money or something, and they came to California, and they bought a ranch. And he was here about, oh, about a week, and he called me up. He was telling me about the... What year would this be about? He was sick. I mean, I was about 42, I think. 42, 42, 43. And he called me up one day. We met, and he said, I said, how are you feeling, Jelly? He said, boy, I'm really coming on real fine. This was just before he died, you know? Just one week before he died. Yeah. And following week, when I got the news that he died... Well, he died, I think, in the summer of 41. Well, 41. In fact, weren't you... Wasn't that when you were playing the show with Duke Ellington here at the Mayan Theater? Yeah, Jump for Joy. Jump for Joy. Yeah. So he must have died during the run of Jump for Joy. I thought it was 41 or 42. It was 41. I think the summer of 41. Mm-hmm. Did you attend his funeral? No, I didn't, because nobody notified me where he was going to be buried or whatnot, you know? Because he was buried right here in Los Angeles. Yeah, I know. But nobody sent... His wife didn't send any invitation or anything like that to let you know what's happening, you know? Because, God, I would have, you know, I would have been there. Sure. And... But he was a real fantastic guy. Let's, just for one second, make sure that we got the volume and everything set right. Let's stop a second. We'll check it out. Good. If we go too far. But, you know, the thing about Jeldy, he was crazy about Omar Simeon. Omar Simeon is one of the unsung heroes of the music. Especially clarinetists. I mean, the guy could really blow them. But he never had the chance because his wife held him back. Was I? Yeah, she did. She really did. Because I tried to get him into Duke's band. And he was all set. That was in New York. And she wanted him to go to Chicago so she could be in society with people, you know? And then when we finally began to travel, we came to Chicago, and the place was back in jam, and here she comes, and she says, hit me. I said, what for? I said, because I didn't listen to you, Simeon got in the band. And that boy, he was fantastic, and a lovely guy. I mean, we'll... Let's get back to Jelly. Now, you mentioned the first time you met Jelly would have been in the Plantation Club about 1925. Right. That's not the first time you heard him play. Oh, yeah. I heard him play, and I was... It was like something out of this world, because he played different than all other pianists. Where would that be? Where was it? That was on 125th Street. I can't think of the name in New York. It was 125th Street. I can't think of the name of the place. You didn't hear him playing in Chicago when you saw him the first time, when you first met him? I made a couple of gigs with him in Chicago. I heard him there, too. When you were with Oliver? Yeah. That or... Before, you see... Here's the thing. I was supposed to work with Oliver at the... What's that? The Royal Garden. Mm-hmm. And the place burned down. So I had to gig. And I finally got a gig with Jelly. Yeah. Yeah. Do you recall much about the band? Well, he had... The type of band he had, who was with him? He had Mitch Miller. You remember Mitch Miller? Mitch Miller? You mean, uh, Mitchell. George Mitchell. George Mitchell. George Mitchell, yeah. Oh, yeah? George Mitchell? Yeah, he was a little humpback guy. Yeah? And, uh... Because he recorded extensively with... Yeah, with Jelly, yeah. And, uh, I think Zudi was there, too. Was there? Yeah. You played, what, just casual dates around Chicago? Just casual, like gigs. We call them gigs, you know. And this would be maybe... One-nighter. 1925, 26? Yeah, just about that time. And then, that's the way I don't know. How big a band would it be, uh, in these gigs? About, uh, ten pieces or something like that. And do you recall if you played, uh, written arrangements, uh, or, uh, or, uh, Mm-hmm . Yeah, we played some, but we played a lot by head, too. Just wondered if Jelly had written-out scores for this band? Mm-hmm . And we were going to do a lot. In those days, we used to have an orchestration. Oh, a stock orchestra? Yeah, a stock orchestration like that. And we followed that, but we'd do what we wanted at that time. Bill seems to be very interested. He's given me a whole section here marked rehearsals to get some of the background and some of the insight. Well, I never. Did you actually rehearse these type of things? Well, we rehearsed his tunes. You did? Yes. We rehearsed his tunes. We'd have a two or three hours rehearsal. Where would you hold rehearsals? Before we recorded. No, no. I mean for these gigs that you played. Oh, no, no. No rehearsal? No. No. The only rehearsal we had was at the Union for his date, for his numbers, his own compositions. For the recording date? Yeah, for recording. That's the only time. All right. Then we'll jump to New York for this 1929 recording date. Yeah. You actually had rehearsals. Oh, yeah. This was just a trio. Yeah, we rehearsed. Did you ever record anything with Morton beside those trio tunes? No, no. Now, we just got through playing those four records, Turtle Twist and Smile Them The Blues Away and My Little Dixie Home and so on. These were recorded, apparently, during the time you were with Ellington. Right. And you were recording extensively with the Duke's band. With the Duke, yeah. But yet, the type of music you were playing with Morton was altogether different than the- Oh, sure. It was completely different. Was there an intent- Were you intentionally making your horn sound different than you did with the Ellington band? Well, I tried to- I tried to suit the mood of Jelliot, what he wanted. See? And I forgot about Ellington when I was working with- Because the work you did with Ellington had a typical Barney Begard, New Orleans sound to it, but yet the clarinet work that you did with Morton was more traditional. Yeah, yeah. It seemed to be going- like you were reaching back- That's it. That's what I was trying to do. I mean, because I knew what the man wanted. And he was like, school me, you know, and tell me what he want done and that was- Well, now at these rehearsals, did he actually tell you how he wanted you to play? No. No, he didn't. He just said, big, do what you want to do. And if he didn't like it, then he would tell me. And I tried my best to try to follow him because I used to listen to Simeon with him, you know, and then I tried to imitate Simeon, you see. Ah, that's probably what it was. Mm-hmm. Now, the reason I questioned the date earlier, when Bill Russell had spoken to Zutty about these same recordings, and of course, musicians are notorious for having a poor memory as far as dates are concerned. Yes, they're right. Zutty thought that maybe these sides- and Zutty was the drummer on those- He was. Yes. Zutty thought that maybe they were made in Chicago, and he remembered that Jelly had waited for you to come to Chicago with Duke to make the records, but of course, as far as the Victor files are concerned, RCA, they put it as a New York date, but you do recall that it was- I think it was New York. Yes. Do you remember the studio, where it was recorded? Mm-hmm . record. Yeah, no, this was a Victor date. Victor, well, Victor was at the, was the same leader grand hall. Was he? Sure. Bill mentions that when he was in New York in the late 30s, and of course this was 10 years later, he visited a studio on 24th Street on the east side, but maybe that's no. Now, here's an interesting point that he wanted to check out. Most of these numbers, these four tunes that you did, well, none of them were recorded again. I mean, they just came and went, but they were published by a man by the name of Harrison Smith. That's a Negro publisher in New York. Did you ever hear of Harrison Smith? Never have. Well, then that would negate any other questions about him. Well, you see, Jelly, all his business was with Melrose. Yes, that was my impression. All his business was with Melrose. Well, he indicates here that some or most of these particular numbers, these particular four, were published by Harrison Smith. Incidentally, it's kind of interesting, this, the titles here, like, for example, Turtle Twist. By today's standard, the twist has become part of our way of life. Yeah. This must have been the first time the twist was used in a song title. That's right. Does it mean anything? What's Turtle Twist mean? He didn't say, he didn't say, he didn't say, because in New Orleans, they got so many turtles, you know, coming out the ground, and they're tristing all over the place, they probably got it from there. But there was no explanation of what the title, what the title was. No, no, no, no. In fact, all of these titles are rather strange. In listening to those four records, I know that you felt it was a long time, a long, many years have passed since we, since you were involved. But is there any question that you made those records? No. It's for sure that this was you? Mm-hmm. Not whatsoever. All right, we're munching a few hors d'oeuvres here, Bill, in case you wonder what the chewing is. But we're having a good time. Four tunes usually comprise a recording session, I guess. At that time, yeah. Do you know if there were any other, did you do any other recording with Morton? No. That was all? That was all I did, because Simeon came to New York, and he started recording with him again. Mm-hmm. Your relationship, as far as these records were concerned, were for just the four tunes. That's right. You mentioned those gigs that you played around Chicago. Did you ever travel with Morton, or play any tours? No, he came to Milwaukee when I was with Charlie Elgar. And Omar Simeon was with Charlie Elgar, too. And he came over there, and he was trying to get a job. But he didn't succeed. Mm-hmm. Because he was a fantastic man. I mean, it's like I told you before, he can talk himself into the job and talk himself right out. Really. Yeah, well, he's an egotistical guy. I guess he offended a lot of people. Wonderful man. All right. Let's see what else Bill would like to hear. Of course, there are a lot of tunes that Jelly is famous for. We mentioned some of them. I just wondered if, in your years with Ellington, at the time you were with Ellington, being a Victor recording artist, Ellington and Morton both recorded for Victor at the same time. And they both had bands on the road. Did you ever discuss Morton with Ellington? Oh, sure. What would Ellington think of a man like Jelly Roll Morton? He thought he was fantastic. He did. He did. You know, the funny thing, and I hate to bring it up because, and Jelly said, he told us that he composed St. Louis Blues. But he had never put it into the publishers. And W.C. Handy got hold of it and took it and made it. He published it and put it in the hands of the publisher. Now, whether it's true or not, I don't know. But he firmly claimed that he wrote it and he said, and even after it was a big standard, you know, he said, I wouldn't do anything in the world to hurt the old man. Hmm. He said, let him take the glory. But I know that Jelly was capable of writing most anything. He had a brilliant mind. And just like I told you, when he wanted money, he would just go out of Melrose, say I won a thousand dollars, two thousand dollars, say I'll send you some tunes. And he'd write them and send it to him. I don't know all the tunes that he's written. He really wrote quite a few. Well, I think if you were to list all of his tunes, it would fill a volume. But maybe just for what it's worth, we mentioned Wolverine Blues and King Porter's Domp and, of course, his Jelly Roll Blues and... Martin Boy Joys. Yeah, and Kansas City Stomps. Grandpa Spells, I'm sure you're familiar with that. The Pearls. Pearls, yeah. Black Bottom Stomp, Mr. Jelly Lord and so on. Were you ever in his home, Barney, or... No, never, never visited him. Did you know his wife? No, he had too many wives. I didn't know the... Did you meet any of his wives or girlfriends? I met the last one. The one out here? Yeah, the one that was out here, but I wouldn't even... Would that be Anita Gonzalez? Pardon me, I think so. That was the one I knew. But then he had another wife in New York, of course. Now, Jelly is supposedly famous, in addition to being a musician, he's famous as a pool shark and a gambler. Did you ever... He was a gambler, a pimp. A pimp, yeah. Everything, I mean... Did you ever see him play pool? No. Did you ever see him gamble? Yeah. What's that name? Koch. Koch? Koch. Was that a card game? Yeah, a card game. Where would that be? In New York? New Orleans. You saw him playing? I just heard about him. He was a good Koch player. Yeah. From my uncle, Emil. When would you say was the last time that you saw him, Morton? Well, just about... just before he died, I mean... Did you see him here in Los Angeles? Yeah. Oh, you did see him when you were... Yeah, I saw him here just a week before he died. All right. Well, that would be about July of 1940. I think he died July 10th, 1941, if I'm not mistaken. Well, I can tell you. He called me. He did. We stayed keeping the, you know... Did you visit him where he was staying? No, he was staying out around Duarte or somewhere. He bought a... his wife bought a ranch or something out there. I see. I don't know if it was Duarte or something, but it's out there anyway. He called, and we talked, and he said, I said, how you getting along? I said, fine. Next week he was gone. Of course, I had the chance to read some of the letters that he wrote from Los Angeles at that time, and it was pretty pathetic. He was in a pretty bad shape. The records that we played were the classic trio, piano, clarinet, and drums. Morton, of course, had used that form earlier on records with Johnny Dodds, with the Jelly Roll Morton trio, and I guess the one that capitalized the most on that same musical form would be the Benny Goodman version. Would you say that a trio like this was something traditional in the New Orleans idiom? Oh, yeah. Bands in New Orleans play this type of music? Yes, but they only used... In New Orleans, they only used six pieces. I mean, they never did have a trio. They didn't know what it was to have a trio, because to the guys, it didn't sound right. You know what I mean? So they had to have six pieces, and that was included, the trumpet, clarinet, trombone, piano, bass, and drums. Well, then, do you think maybe Morton innovated, invented the idea? I think so. Yeah? I think so. Because you take nowadays, I mean, everywhere you go is nothing but trios or something like that. Piano, guitar, bass, or whatever it is, you know. Mm-hmm. Or drums. It's only three pieces. Everywhere you go, that's all you find is a trio. Well, today in the cocktail lounge, there's something to do. And maybe this was another thing that Jelly was instrumental in starring. I thought perhaps it was something that he had... But that doesn't make music, though. A trio doesn't make music, unless you've got three outstanding people to do this thing. And, you know, they got to be above the average, in other words, to make this kind of music. All right, let's go back to New Orleans in the early days when you said you heard about Morton. You never saw, actually saw Jelly when you were living in New Orleans. No, no. You were younger than him, of course, so you wouldn't have gotten around. Well, my uncle used to, he was a fiddle player, he used to play with Kid O'Ree. What was his name? Emile Bigard. Mm-hmm. And he used to talk about Jelly all the time. You know, Jelly was working for Lulu White, which the woman I told you before that. Mm-hmm, yeah. Mahogany, huh? The house of ill repute. Yeah. And he used to talk because Jelly would make more money than all them characters. Mm-hmm. Because, you know, the guys tip him to, you know. And Jelly was... Well, did Emile work with Jelly? No. He just knew him. He knew him real. Yeah. Jelly was like a, what you would say, a loner. Mm-hmm. Because he made more money than all these characters put together. Because he's working at his house, and his tips was more than what these guys would get for a whole week. Mm-hmm. See, and I knew that. And his sister, you know, you mentioned his sister before. She was crazy about Albert Nicholas. That's Francis? Yeah. She was crazy about Albert Nicholas. That's all right. Mm-hmm. And they used to go together. What about the way Jelly would dress? Was there anything particular about his... He was immaculate. Oh, yeah. He was immaculate, man. Oh. And he'd like... He would love to grin to show that diamond in his tooth. How about these periods when he was down, when he was... Well, that was the pathetic part of it. When he couldn't, you know, couldn't get the clothes that he wanted, and he was kind of sad. And he luck... Luckily, he got this woman that little money, and he came out to California, and he bought the place. But he didn't know it. I think we just about covered all of the points. Where, except maybe some just personal opinions, without trying to be flattering. After all, we're not here to flatter Morton. If there's anything derogatory, we'd bring that up, too. Where would you put him on a basis of values in the world of jazz? We all look like Louis Armstrong might be up near the top or at the top. How would you evaluate? How important is him? Jelly was a... I'll say he was a pioneer of jazz. You know, I mean, but... A lot of people, a lot of musicians try to copy his style. He had something. He had to have something. If you had to rank the five top jazz personalities of all time, would you say Jelly would be one of those? I should say so. I would, really. And... P. Ron had another guy who was... Steve. His first name was Steve. I can't think of him. Steve Lewis. Uh-huh. And he was quite a guy, but he never did get the recognition that Jelly got, you know, of course. He played piano? Yeah. And he was in P. Ron's band, Orchestra. Well, I guess Jelly's greatness was the fact that not only he played piano, but he composed. Yeah. And he had a ring. That's the thing. And it's two different categories, you know. Because P. Ron was like a society band. Jelly was a hunky-tonk man. You know, and the people went more for hunky-tonk than they went for A.J. P. Ron. Well, how would you compare, for example, as on a stature basis, as far as their greatness, Morton with Ellington? Since they're both composers, they're both band leaders. There's two different types. Well, let's just say up until the time Morton died, up until 1941, because Ellington has gone on beyond there. Oh, I think Jelly was above him at that time. Do you really? Sure. Jelly was above him. But as the years progressed, I mean, Ellington surpassed him. Yes, because there's been many years involved. But I think Jelly wrote more damn tunes than Ellington ever thought about writing. Because I often think of the two as being parallel. They're both great composers, great arrangers. Sure. Was there anybody else that you can recall who actually arranged and wrote parts for a New Orleans sound, as Morton did? No. I think, uh, what's the kid used to be with, uh, Crosby? Matty Matlock. Matty Matlock, yes. Matty Matlock and, uh, the, uh, the tenor man. Eddie Miller? Eddie Miller. Of course Matty wasn't, isn't arranged. Uh-huh. But I think both of them, uh, did the job, uh, well, real well. Because when Crosby had, remember, he had this band? Bobcats. Bobcats. And they played strictly New Orleans. Of course Matty was probably drawing on things he had heard Morton do. Sure. All right. Uh, the tape has just got a few seconds more. As I just take the microphone and tell me anything that comes to mind that you, uh, might add about Jelly? Well, all right. All I can say, I think that Jelly's one of the greatest. I mean, and he should be in the Hall of Fame at all times. And, and eventually he will be in there. Oh, he is in there already. I'm sure he is. Sure. And it's going to be the same thing with Louis Armstrong. If anything should happen to him, he's going to be in there too. We'll, like W.C. Handy, you know. And then, that's what's going to happen. You, you can't, uh, put the man down, period. And I loved him. And I really respected him, period. And God bless his soul. Okay. Okay. Thank you, Barney. Hi, Bill. Uh, this should give you all the information you need. If there's anything else, uh, that we can help. Oh, yeah. One more thing. Barney, so that Bill will know. Where do I find this here? Just a minute. Or is it? Well, temporarily I don't find it. But I have a check here that he gave me to give you. Here we go. Signed by William Russell. Hello. Made out. Wonderful. For the sum of $25, which, uh, you're going to receive now. And this gives Bill the right to all of the material that, uh, you've just provided. And he's going to ask you to sign this little form here. Will do. This is going to be for a book that he's doing, uh, about Jelly Roll Morton, of course. Uh, not for profit, I assure you. Uh, this is a labor of love. I'm sorry. But, um, I told him when I saw you, saw him in New Orleans, that money wasn't important for a thing like this. But he insisted that you accept this check. So I'm going to give it to you. Thank you. And, uh, we'll go on from here. Well, thank you. Give me some more of them, John. Okay. Thank you.
. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. That's okay. You can cut that off. One. Two. You see, if you count and then pick back the notes up, it screws you up. Yeah. ¶ Thank you.

I don't know. I think it's good. Yeah. Try it again. Where do you want that drum to come in? Right on the front. Yeah, he come in on the second beat between the trumpets. No, I'll come in. I'll come in for a different first time. See, we got the dance set. Yeah, I'll do one. Two.

segments.title: Bigard on Jelly Roll Morton: 1929 trio session, Chicago gigs, character, legacy
segments.summary: Floyd Levin interviews Bigard for Bill Russell about Jelly Roll Morton: dating the Victor trio session, meeting Morton in Chicago c.1925, his publisher Melrose, his death in 1941, the trio format, and Bigard's ranking of him against Ellington.

segments.title: Tape noise and studio chatter after the interview
segments.summary: Garbled recording with repeated 'thank you', a count-in and brief musicians' talk about a drum entrance.
